name: Embryolisse Lait-Crème Concentré

card.summary: A French multi-purpose moisturising cream used by makeup artists as a hydrating base under makeup for smoother-looking skin.
card.note: Rich formula; people with oily, combination or sensitive skin may react to individual ingredients.

quick.overview:
Embryolisse Lait-Crème Concentré is a rich, light-textured cream from the French brand Embryolisse, known as a long-standing staple in makeup artists' kits. It is used as a daily moisturiser and as a hydrating layer under foundation.

The appearance payoff is skin that looks softer and more even before makeup, so base products sit smoothly. Its reputation rests on makeup artist use, brand history and consumer reviews rather than published clinical trials.
quick.how: People apply it to clean skin as a moisturiser, massage it in before makeup as a primer, use it as a mask, a makeup remover or refresher, or as an aftershave balm. It is usually part of a simple routine with cleanser and sunscreen.
quick.risks: As a cosmetic cream it can irritate people with sensitivities. Beaut.ie notes it is not ideal as a daily moisturiser for combination or oily skin and suggests avoiding the T-zone when used as a primer on shiny skin.

lead: Embryolisse Lait-Crème Concentré is a multi-purpose moisturising cream from the French brand Embryolisse. It was formulated in 1950 by a dermatologist at Saint-Louis Hospital in Paris, and the brand says it was first prescribed by doctors before becoming a cult product in French pharmacies.[1] It is widely described as a makeup artists' staple.[3][4]

People use it for a smoother, softer, more hydrated look: as a moisturiser, as a primer under foundation so makeup sits without pilling or separating, and as an overnight or rehydrating mask.[2][3] Makeup artist Olivier Tissot, in brand material, says it can be massaged into skin to relax it before makeup and absorbs quickly.[4]
Coverage of the product is mostly editorial, retail and brand material. Its main ingredients are shea butter, beeswax, soy proteins and aloe vera.[2][4]

chain: Cream is massaged into clean skin
Foundation applies more smoothly and skin looks dewy
angle.text: It moisturises and prepares skin so makeup applies evenly, and some people use it to soothe dry or irritated patches. The effect is on hydration and surface texture.

infobox: 1950, by a dermatologist at Saint-Louis Hospital, Paris
Shea butter, beeswax, soy proteins, aloe vera

paras: The brand markets the cream as a 6-in-1 product and sells it in more than 50 countries.[1] Retail and editorial coverage describes uses as a moisturiser, makeup primer, night cream, soothing product for redness and irritation, hydration mask, makeup remover, makeup refresher (buffed onto dry patches of foundation) and aftershave balm.[2][3]

Beaut.ie describes the texture as light and fluid and says it is not ideal as an everyday moisturiser for combination or oily skin; it also advises avoiding the T-zone when using it as a primer if skin gets shiny.[3]

Embryolisse says it was founded in 1950 by a dermatologist and is now a family-owned French company run by a pharmacist and his wife. The formula, according to the brand, has changed little since the 1950s.[1][2] In 2022 the brand reports working with makeup artists on more than 75 film, television and event productions in France.[1]

In the 2010s and 2020s the cream was promoted in beauty media through makeup artist endorsements, a mention of model Karlie Kloss praising it in 2009, and viral interest after a makeup artist on the Netflix series Emily in Paris reportedly used it on Lily Collins.[2]

No safety issues specific to the product have been reported beyond general cosmetic-cream cautions: shea butter, beeswax and soy ingredients may not suit everyone, and richer creams can feel heavy on oily or acne-prone skin.[2][3]

timeline.event: A dermatologist at Saint-Louis Hospital formulates the cream; the brand dates its founding to the same year.[1]
Model Karlie Kloss praises the cream in press coverage.[2]
Embryolisse reports partnering with makeup artists on more than 75 shoots and events in France.[1]
BuzzFeed News publishes a popularity roundup noting its place in the TikTok skin flooding trend.[2]

lore.intro: Online and in beauty media, the cream is discussed as a cheap pharmacy product that makeup artists favour and shoppers use for several purposes.[2]

claims.claim: It makes foundation sit smoothly as a primer
claims.believers: Amazon reviewers quoted by BuzzFeed say it keeps makeup from pilling or separating and hydrates without greasiness.[2]
claims.experts: No published studies have tested it as a primer; makeup artists in brand and editorial material describe it as preparing skin for makeup.[3][4]

claims.claim: It soothes sensitive, dry or flaky skin
claims.believers: Reviewers and the BuzzFeed author, who has dry, sensitive skin, report calmer, more comfortable skin.[2]
claims.experts: No clinical trials of the product have been published; the accounts are anecdotal.

claims.claim: It fits into TikTok's "skin flooding" routine
claims.believers: Coverage links the cream to the skin flooding trend, which layers hydrating products on damp skin.[2]
claims.experts: No published studies examine this product in such routines.
